etymologies.etymologyHTML: Verb from Middle English scornen, schornen, alteration of Old French escharnir, from Vulgar Latin *escarnire, from Proto-Germanic *skarnjan, which could be from *skeraną (“to shear”) (from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”)), or possibly related to *skarną (“dung, filth”) (from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱerd-, *(s)ḱer- (“dung, manure, filth”)). Noun from Old French escarn (cognate with Portuguese escárnio, Spanish escarnio and Italian scherno).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To feel or display contempt or disdain for something or somebody; to despise.

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene v], page 150:
quote.text: The Cry is ſtill, they come: our Caſtles ſtrength / Will laugh a Siedge to ſcorne
We scorn what is in itself contemptible or disgraceful.

quote.citation: 1697, [William] Congreve, The Mourning Bride, a Tragedy. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, Act III, page 39:
quote.text: Heav'n has no Rage, like Love to Hatred turn'd, / Nor Hell a Fury, like a Woman ſcorn'd.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To refuse to do something, as beneath oneself.

quote.citation: 1578–1579, Ed[mund] Sp[enser], “Prosopopoia. Or Mother Hubberds Tale. [...] Dedicated to the Right Honorable the Ladie Compton and Mountegle”, in Complaints. Containing Sundrie Small Poemes of the Worlds Vanitie. Whereof the Next Page Maketh Mention‎[1], London: Imprinted for William Ponsonbie, dwelling in Paules Churchyard at the signe of the Bishops head, published 1591, →OCLC:
quote.text: For miſerie doth braueſt mindes abate, / And make them ſeeke for that they wont to ſcorne, / Of fortune and of hope at once forlorne.

quote.citation: 1967, John Berryman, Berryman’s Sonnets, New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux:
quote.text: Rain of tears, real, mist of imagined scorn

definitions.definition: (countable) A display of disdain; a slight.

quote.citation: 1591 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The First Part of Henry the Sixt”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene vi], page 100, column 1:
quote.text: VVith ſcoffes and ſcornes, and contumelious taunts, / In open Market-place produc't they me, / To be a publique ſpectacle to all: / Here, ſayd they, is the Terror of the French, / The Scar-Crovv that affrights our Children ſo.
Every sullen frown and bitter scorn / But fanned the fuel that too fast did burn.

definitions.definition: (countable) An object of disdain, contempt, or derision.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Psalms 44:13:
quote.text: Thou makest us a reproach to our neighbours, a scorn and a derision to them that are round about us.
